lead: The OSI reference model splits every job a network must do into seven layers, from bits on a cable at the bottom to the user's application at the top. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) built it in the 1980s so that designers, vendors and examiners could talk about one layer at a time. It is a model, not software: it names jobs and the interfaces between them but defines no headers. Its vocabulary — layer 2 switch, layer 3 routing, layer 4 port — is used every day by network engineers.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.4 for protocols, encapsulation and the idea of a PDU (protocol data unit): the chunk of data a layer hands down.

sections.h3: A model, not a protocol suite

blocks.text: A reference model is a template. It says which jobs exist and how they stack, so that any vendor can build compliant hardware and software that talks to another vendor's product. The OSI model defines seven layers. Each layer has exactly one job, serves the layer above it, and is served by the layer below it.

The boundary between two adjacent layers is an interface. It is a contract: the upper layer passes a data unit plus its own control information down, and it never needs to know how the lower layer does its work. Layer N on the sender adds its header and logically talks to layer N on the receiver, using that header. This is encapsulation, and the whole stack is peeled open at the far end.

Each layer names its data unit. From the bottom: bits at the physical layer, a frame at the data link layer, a packet at the network layer, a segment (or datagram, for UDP) at the transport layer, and simply data or a message above that.

Because the model is generic, it fits a phone call, a satellite link or a bank's private network. That generality is also its weakness: it is descriptive, so it can be read as vague. A real product is built from a protocol suite, which is a set of protocols that actually run. OSI, as a suite, lost to TCP/IP; OSI, as a teaching model, won everywhere.

sections.h3: The seven layers, from the wire up

items: 1 Physical. Moves single bits over a medium: voltage, light, radio, pin layout, data rate. PDU: bit. Examples: RS-232, the 1000BASE-T cable spec. Devices: hub, repeater, cable, connector.

2 Data link. Delivers a chunk of data across one link to the next node. Frames the bits, adds MAC addresses, detects errors with a trailer, controls access to a shared medium. PDU: frame. Examples: Ethernet, HDLC, PPP. Devices: switch, bridge.
3 Network. Delivers a packet from the source host to the destination host across many links. Logical addressing and routing are its job. PDU: packet. Examples: IP, ICMP. Device: router.

4 Transport. End-to-end delivery of the whole message between two processes. Adds port numbers, splits data into segments, and may add retransmission and flow control. PDU: segment. Examples: TCP, UDP. Runs inside the host operating system, not on a box in the corridor.
5 Session. Sets up, manages and closes a dialogue between two applications: who speaks when, and checkpoints so a long transfer can resume after a break. PDU: data.
6 Presentation. Fixes the syntax of the data so both sides read the same bytes: character encoding, compression, encryption. PDU: data.
7 Application. The network services a user program calls: web pages, mail, name lookup. PDU: data. Examples: HTTP, SMTP, DNS.

blocks.text: The upper three layers (5, 6, 7) are called the upper layers and live in software near the application. The lower four (1 to 4) are called the lower layers; layers 1 and 2 live in the network card, and layer 3 lives in the operating system and in routers. Your exam will mostly test layers 2, 3 and 4, so learn those cold and know the other four by one sentence each.

sections.h3: Mapping to TCP/IP, and the standard criticism

blocks.text: The Internet does not run OSI. It runs the TCP/IP suite, which has four layers: network access, internet, transport, and application. Map the two like this. OSI physical and data link fold into TCP/IP network access. OSI network maps to the internet layer. OSI transport maps to transport. OSI session, presentation and application all collapse into the single TCP/IP application layer. Unit 2 covers the full suite.

That collapse is the standard criticism of OSI. Session and presentation are thin in real software: a browser or a mail client does checkpoints and encodings itself, using library calls, so no separate layer exists to hand data to. TLS encryption, for example, is usually drawn beside the application rather than as a presentation layer.

Two more criticisms worth one line each. The model was written before the protocols that won, so the fit is loose. And its seven layers were once said to be a political number rather than a technical one. Keep the model anyway: it gives each job exactly one home, and that is why we still argue about which layer a firewall or a load balancer belongs to.

spec.aria: The seven OSI layers stacked from application to physical, with the bytes each adds and the size after it: 1200, 1200, 1200, 1220, 1240, 1258 and 1258.

examples.question: An application in host A produces 1200 bytes of user data, and the 1200 bytes already include the application-layer header. The data goes down a full OSI stack. The transport layer adds a 20-byte header, the network layer adds a 20-byte header, and the data link layer adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte trailer. The session and presentation layers add nothing. Find the size of the segment, the packet and the frame, the total overhead in bytes, and the protocol efficiency as a percentage.
steps: Transport layer: it takes 1200 bytes and appends 20 bytes. Segment size = 1200 + 20 = 1220 bytes.
Network layer: it takes the 1220-byte segment and appends 20 bytes. Packet size = 1220 + 20 = 1240 bytes.
Data link layer: it takes the 1240-byte packet, adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte trailer. Frame size = 1240 + 14 + 4 = 1258 bytes.
Efficiency = useful bytes ÷ bytes on the wire = 1200 ÷ 1258 = 0.9539, that is 95.39 percent.
examples.answer: The frame is 1258 bytes on the wire, 58 bytes are overhead, and the protocol efficiency is 95.39 percent.
examples.check:
app = 1200
seg = app + 20
pkt = seg + 20
frame = pkt + 14 + 4
oh = frame - app
eff = app / frame * 100
print(seg)
print(pkt)
print(frame)
print(oh)
print(round(eff, 2))

traps: Calling OSI a protocol suite. It is a reference model and defines no headers, ports or field layouts of its own.
Putting encryption in the transport layer. Encryption is presentation; TCP's job is end-to-end delivery with ports and retransmission.
Putting routing in the data link layer. A switch forwards frames by MAC address within one network; a router forwards packets by IP address between networks.
Saying the session layer is where a TCP connection is made. TCP connections belong to transport; session is about the application dialogue.
Forgetting the trailer. Data link overhead is header plus trailer, and one mark is lost by counting the header alone.

quiz.q: Name the seven OSI layers in order from layer 1 upward, and give the PDU of each of the bottom four.
quiz.a: Physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application. PDUs: bit, frame, packet, segment.

quiz.q: Why does each layer need to know only its own header and not the headers above it?
quiz.a: Because of the interface contract. Layer N receives a payload from layer N+1 and treats everything inside it as opaque data. On arrival, the peer layer N reads and strips its own header and passes the rest up. This lets any layer be replaced without touching the others, which is the whole point of layering.

quiz.q: Name the OSI layer for each task. (a) Encrypting a file before sending. (b) Choosing a route across three routers. (c) Retransmitting a lost segment. (d) Turning bits into an electrical signal. (e) Keeping a user logged in across many requests. (f) Adding port numbers. (g) Adding a MAC address and a check trailer.
quiz.a: (a) presentation, (b) network, (c) transport, (d) physical, (e) session, (f) transport, (g) data link.

quiz.q: A 500-byte message is sent down a stack where transport adds 20 bytes, network adds 20 bytes, and data link adds 18 bytes in total. Find the frame size, the overhead and the efficiency.
quiz.a: Segment = 500 + 20 = 520 bytes. Packet = 520 + 20 = 540 bytes. Frame = 540 + 18 = 558 bytes. Overhead = 58 bytes. Efficiency = 500 / 558 = 89.6 percent.

quiz.q: OSI has separate session and presentation layers, but TCP/IP does not. Give two reasons why the collapse happened and one cost of it.
quiz.a: First, real software does these jobs inside the application process with library calls, so there is no separate entity to hand data to. Second, the model was written before the winning protocols, so its layer count reflects design intent rather than deployed code. The cost is that encryption and encoding logic is repeated in every application instead of being reusable at one layer, which makes it harder to reason about security in one place.

quiz.q: A firewall reads TCP port numbers, and a switch reads MAC addresses. State the highest OSI layer each device reaches and why a router needs more than the switch does.
quiz.a: The switch works up to layer 2, because a frame's MAC header is enough to forward within one network. The firewall reaches layer 4, because the port number is in the transport header. A router must reach layer 3: it has to read the destination IP address and consult a routing table to choose the next network, which a MAC address alone cannot tell it.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a reference model and a protocol suite?
quiz.a: A reference model is a template that names jobs and the interfaces between them; it specifies no headers, so it cannot run. A protocol suite is a set of concrete protocols with defined header formats and procedures that actually run on hosts and routers. OSI is the model; TCP/IP is the suite the Internet uses.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engineers still use the layer number as shorthand for the kind of device or the kind of fault: layer 1 problem means a bad cable, layer 3 problem means a routing loop. Cloud providers now sell layer 4 and layer 7 load balancers as distinct products, which is OSI vocabulary turned into prices. Software-defined networking keeps the layers but moves the control decisions to a central program, so the interesting research is about where the layer boundary should sit. Search next for encapsulation, overlay networks, and the service mesh idea that puts session-like logic back into software.
